paragraphs.heading: Seeing inside with vibrations
paragraphs.text: A seismic wave is a mechanical wave, a travelling vibration of acoustic energy, that moves through Earth or another planet. Earthquakes make them, but so can volcanic eruptions, moving magma, big landslides and large human-made explosions. Seismologists record these waves with seismometers, hydrophones in water, or accelerometers. In geophysics, the way the waves bend and bounce back is used to study Earth's internal structure.

paragraphs.heading: Why the waves change speed
paragraphs.text: How fast a seismic wave travels depends on the kind of wave and on the density and elasticity of the rock it crosses. Waves passing through the interior follow paths set by the rock's density and stiffness. Those properties in turn change with temperature, composition and phase. The bending of these paths is much like the way light bends.

paragraphs.heading: Body waves and surface waves
paragraphs.text: There is a broad split between body waves, which pass through the inside of the Earth, and surface waves, which run along its surface. Surface waves fade more slowly with distance and shake the ground harder, so they tend to do more damage. Body waves come in two kinds, primary and secondary, a split the French mathematician Siméon Denis Poisson recognized in 1830.

paragraphs.heading: Primary and secondary waves
paragraphs.text: Primary waves, or P waves, are compression waves of the longitudinal kind. They are the fastest, so they reach recording stations first, and they can cross any material, liquids included. Secondary waves, or S waves, shake the ground sideways, at right angles to their path. They arrive later, usually travel at about 60% of the P wave speed, and can move only through solids.

paragraphs.heading: What the waves reveal
paragraphs.text: Because different wave types travel at different speeds, the gaps between their arrival times let scientists pinpoint where an earthquake began. The waves also show how the planet is built. Their speed generally rises with depth through the crust and mantle, then falls sharply at the outer core. S waves do not appear in the outer core, and since they cannot cross liquid, this suggests the outer core is liquid.

paragraphs.heading: Probing shallow ground
paragraphs.text: Scientists do not always wait for a quake. Sometimes they make vibrations themselves and measure them to look at structures close beneath the surface. Seismic waves also have to be told apart from seismic noise, the constant faint shaking that comes from many natural and human sources.
